problem: Existing embodied benchmarks focus on short-horizon navigation or manipulation with fixed task categories (Behavior-1K uses predefined goals), so they do not test long-horizon planning, memory, dependency management and self-improvement under free-form instructions. VLM agents also lack architectures that stay stable over thousands of steps.
motivation: Real household routines are compound, implicitly ordered, and require memory, re-planning and learning from mistakes over hundreds of human steps. Naive VLM deployment collapses over such horizons, so the paper asks whether agent structure, rather than parameter scale alone, drives long-horizon success.
key_idea: Build LongAct, a 300-episode free-form long-horizon household benchmark on ProcTHOR/AI2-THOR with an Improvement Rate metric, and HoloMind, a zero-shot VLM agent combining DAG hierarchical planning, multimodal spatial memory, episodic memory and a global Critic.
insight: Agent structure matters more than scale: Qwen3-VL-32B goes from 6.14 GC as a pure VLM to 51.2 GC under HoloMind, and the 32B/8B gap shrinks from about 8x to about 2x. Ablations show the Critic is the most important module (removing it drops GC 51.2→29.2 and IR 1.64→0.16, with manipulation steps rising 28.7→222). Episodic memory mainly improves efficiency (navigation steps rise 1692→2221 without it) rather than accuracy. Upgrading only the Low-level Planner from 8B to 32B gives the largest gain (GC 24.5→42.8). Errors stay dominated by execution (46.3%) even with GT perception.
method: DAG high-level planner: decomposes the free-form instruction into a goal DAG with dependencies, runs independent goals in parallel, prioritizes spatially close goals, and refines each next sub-instruction using episodic memory so it is self-contained.
Low-level planner: for each refined goal, retrieves the needed objects from spatial memory and otherwise generates search or receptacle-exploration subgoals; incorporates Critic feedback.
Executor: a VLM Translator that selects and composes navigation and manipulation skill-library functions mapped to atomic simulator actions, with lightweight self-recovery.

Multimodal Spatial Memory: a 3D semantic map plus an object-centric database (multi-view RGB, voxels, masks, labels) with spatial and CLIP semantic indices; new objects are merged with matching entries, and top-k retrieval is verified by a VLM over the stored views.
Episodic Memory: Status (held object, position), History (completed subgoals), and Experience (reusable rules and priors) that inform planning.
Critic: at each step issues Pass, Refine or Replan with textual diagnostics; keeps an experience pool of failures and fixes and distills them into episodic memory.

setting.backbone: GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-VL-2B/8B/32B (frozen, prompted), plus CLIP for memory
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus GT semantic segmentation
setting.action_space: low-level ALFRED-style: 8 navigation actions (MoveAhead/Back/Left/Right, Rotate, Look, 0.05 m / 30°) and 7 manipulation actions (Pick/Place, Open/Close, ToggleOn/Off, Slice), Stop; 16,000 step cap
setting.privileged: GT depth and semantic segmentation provided as observations

numbers_note: LongAct is the paper's own benchmark with no official split names; 'test' is used as a placeholder. Table 4 gives SR 2.80 for Qwen3-VL-8B vs 3.00 in Table 1. Human-tester reference: GC 92.9, SR 66.7.
results: On LongAct's detailed split, HoloMind with GPT-5 reaches 59.0 GC and 16.0 SR versus 92.9 GC and 66.7 SR for humans. HoloMind with Qwen3-VL-32B reaches 51.2 GC, versus 6.14 GC for the pure Qwen3-VL-32B VLM. Concise instructions are much harder (16.2 GC, 1.0 SR).
limitations: Planning is reactive: agents revise only after failures and do not actively seek information, so concise-instruction performance is very low (SR 1.0).
Manipulation and execution errors dominate (46.3%) and full-task SR is still low (max 16%), far below humans (66.7%).

Only a single agent architecture family and Qwen3-VL/GPT-5 backbones are evaluated, with no other agent baselines, and the abstraction relies on GT perception and skill libraries rather than real control.
